title: TCP Extensions for High Performance
summary: This document specifies TCP extensions for paths with large bandwidth-delay products and very fast links. It defines the Window Scale option, which allows much larger receive windows, and the Timestamps option, used for round-trip time measurement and for protecting against old, delayed segments. It revises RFC 1323.

eli5.summary: Sending data far away is like filling a long pipe, and you need to keep lots of water in it at once. This RFC lets computers announce a much bigger bucket and stamp each message with a clock.

questions: how does tcp handle high bandwidth delay paths
what is the tcp window scale option
what is the tcp timestamps option
subtitle: Two TCP options, Window Scale and Timestamps, that keep TCP fast and safe on very fast, long-delay paths.

tldr.problem: TCP's 16-bit window field caps the receive window at 64 KiB, and its 32-bit sequence numbers can wrap around within a segment's lifetime on very fast paths, letting old duplicates be mistaken for new data.
tldr.mechanism: The Window Scale option applies a shift count to the window field to allow much larger windows. The Timestamps option carries a clock value in every segment, used for round-trip time measurement (RTTM) and for rejecting old duplicates (PAWS).
tldr.outcome: Together they let TCP fill long, fat paths and stay reliable at very high speeds. RFC 7323 revises and obsoletes RFC 1323, and states that a modern TCP stack is recommended to implement them.

today: RFC 7323 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 1323. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, so it is the current definition of the Window Scale and Timestamps options.

sections.title: Two Problems on Fast, Long Paths
sections.content:
TCP was designed to work over almost any transmission medium, but the fastest paths are now well beyond what it was first engineered for. RFC 7323 defines a set of modest extensions that widen the range where TCP works well. It updates and obsoletes RFC 1323, and the RFC recommends that a modern TCP stack implements and uses the extensions.

The RFC names two core problems on paths with a large bandwidth * delay product, which it calls a long, fat network (LFN). First, the TCP header reports the receive window in a 16-bit field, so the largest window is 2^16, or 64 KiB. When the bandwidth * delay product exceeds that, the window limits throughput. Second, the 32-bit sequence number can wrap within the time a segment lingers in queues, so an old duplicate could be accepted as valid data. Wrap-around can happen once at least 4 GiB are sent in one session.

Both fixes are TCP options. Loss recovery on LFNs is a third issue, but the RFC leaves it to the Selective Acknowledgment documents and does not discuss it further.
sections.eli5: Imagine a very long hose. A tiny bucket at the end means the hose is never full, and old water that got stuck could slosh out later and be mistaken for new water. This RFC fixes both.

sections.title: The Window Scale Option
sections.content:
The Window Scale option (kind 3, length 3 bytes) expands the TCP window to 30 bits. It does this by carrying a shift count, shift.cnt, that tells the peer how many bits to shift the 16-bit window field. A sender right-shifts its true receive window by that count before putting it in the header, and the receiver left-shifts the field it reads.

The option is only sent in SYN segments, so the scale is fixed in each direction when the connection opens. It is an offer, not a promise: both sides MUST send the option in their SYN segments to enable scaling in either direction. A reply in the SYN,ACK may only be sent if the option arrived in the initial SYN. The window field of a SYN segment itself MUST NOT be scaled, and the option in a non-SYN segment MUST be ignored.

The shift count MUST be limited to 14, which allows a maximum window of 1 GiB (2^30). If a larger value is received, the TCP SHOULD log the error but MUST use 14. The limit keeps the sender's and receiver's windows from being confused as old or new data.

Because scaling works in coarse steps, a receiver can end up advertising a window that appears to shrink. Implementations MUST handle a shrinking window as RFC 1122 specifies. The receiver MUST honor any segment that would have been in window for any acknowledgment it sent, and a sender may retransmit out-of-window data under limited conditions.
sections.eli5: Instead of counting in ones, the two computers agree to count in big steps, like counting by 1,000s. That way a small number on the label can stand for a very big bucket.

sections.title: The Timestamps Option
sections.content:
The Timestamps option (kind 8, length 10 bytes) carries two four-byte fields. TSval holds the current value of the sender's timestamp clock. TSecr echoes a recently received TSval from the peer, and it is only valid when the ACK bit is set. When the ACK bit is clear, the sender SHOULD set it to zero and the receiver MUST ignore it.

A TCP MAY send the option in an initial SYN, and MAY send it in the SYN,ACK only if it received one. Once both SYN segments carry it, the option MUST be sent in every non-RST segment for the rest of the connection, and SHOULD be sent in an RST. If a non-RST segment arrives without it, a TCP SHOULD silently drop the segment, but MUST NOT abort the connection for that reason.

The option adds 10 bytes (up to 12 including padding) to the 20-byte TCP header. The RFC notes that the benefit of extra round-trip samples is small, but other uses, namely PAWS and the Eifel mechanism, improve security and performance, so the extra header cost should be weighed against that gain.
sections.eli5: Every message gets a little clock reading stamped on it, and the reply repeats back the last reading it saw. Both sides keep doing this so they can tell how old things are.

sections.title: Measuring Round-Trip Time with RTTM
sections.content:
The first use of timestamps is round-trip time measurement (RTTM). The difference between the current timestamp clock and a received TSecr gives the round-trip time (RTT) of nearly every acknowledged segment, which TCP uses mainly to set its retransmission timeout (RTO).

Not every TSecr is safe to use. If one side pauses sending, the echoed value would include the pause and inflate the RTT. The RTTM Rule therefore says a TSecr MAY be used to update the averaged RTT only if the segment advances the left edge of the send window (SND.UNA increases).

Which TSval to echo depends on the situation. With delayed ACKs, the receiver SHOULD echo the earliest unacknowledged segment. For an out-of-order segment, an ACK SHOULD carry the timestamp of the most recent segment that advanced RCV.NXT. When a segment fills a hole, its own timestamp MUST be echoed. One algorithm covers all three cases using two 32-bit state variables: TS.Recent and Last.ACK.sent. A new TSval is copied to TS.Recent only if SEG.TSval >= TS.Recent and SEG.SEQ <= Last.ACK.sent.

The RFC also warns that the RTO estimator of RFC 6298 assumes at most one sample per RTT. With timestamps, an implementation SHOULD try to keep to the spirit of that history, and Appendix G gives a suggestion.
sections.eli5: If you note the time when you shout and the time the echo comes back, you know how far away the wall is. The only trick is to ignore echoes that were delayed just because you stopped talking for a while.

sections.title: PAWS: Rejecting Old Duplicates
sections.content:
Protection Against Wrapped Sequences (PAWS) uses the same timestamps to reject old duplicate segments within one connection. It assumes the timestamps of received segments are monotonically non-decreasing, and treats a segment whose SEG.TSval is less than TS.Recent as an old duplicate. Timestamps are 32-bit unsigned values compared the same way as sequence numbers. The receiver treats them as a logical extension of the high-order bits of the sequence number, so no clock synchronization between the two ends is needed.

For a synchronized connection, the basic algorithm runs on every incoming segment, before the normal acceptability check:

  • R1: if the segment has a Timestamps option, SEG.TSval < TS.Recent, TS.Recent is valid and RST is not set, send an acknowledgment and drop it.
  • R2: if outside the window, reject it as normal.
  • R3: if SEG.TSval >= TS.Recent and SEG.SEQ <= Last.ACK.sent, record the timestamp in TS.Recent.
  • R4 and R5: accept an in-sequence segment normally; otherwise treat it as an ordinary in-window, out-of-sequence segment.

The timestamp is checked only when a segment first arrives, so data already queued behind a lost segment is not rejected when the retransmission fills the hole. An RST MUST NOT be subjected to the PAWS check.

The clock has limits on both sides. It MUST tick at least once for each 2^31 bytes sent, and its recycle time MUST be greater than the MSL. The RFC chooses a clock frequency in the range 1 ms to 1 sec per tick. Because a connection idle for more than 24 days could freeze under PAWS, implementations must include a way to invalidate TS.Recent after that. Any TCP that implements PAWS MUST also implement Path MTU Discovery, because fragmentation errors at high rates can defeat PAWS and the fix is to set the Don't Fragment bit.
sections.eli5: If each letter carries a date stamp, the mailroom can throw out any letter older than the newest one already seen. A letter that was delayed for ages gets spotted and tossed instead of confusing everyone.

sections.title: Security and Middleboxes
sections.content:
A larger window makes it easier for an attacker to forge a packet that falls inside it. Timestamps and PAWS can help, but a forged packet with a timestamp far in the future could cause valid segments to be dropped by the PAWS check, so implementers should not open the window much beyond what the connection needs. The RFC points to RFC 5961 for mitigations against blind in-window attacks.

A timestamp clock derived straight from system uptime can leak information, so the RFC RECOMMENDS a random, per-connection offset. It also notes that the combination, order and padding of the options can help fingerprint a system.

Some middleboxes are known to strip these options. Removing Window Scale from a SYN,ACK breaks the negotiation, and a stateful firewall that ignores the scale factor cannot judge whether a segment is in the window. Removing Timestamps leaves high-speed connections without PAWS protection.

The RFC adds that, because it makes the rules for a missing Timestamps option explicit, it may reveal middlebox behavior that was previously undetected.
sections.eli5: Bigger buckets are easier for a trickster to toss fake letters into, so computers should not make them bigger than needed. And any helper in the middle who erases the date stamps can break the system.

sections.title: What Changed from RFC 1323
sections.content:
RFC 7323 keeps the two options introduced by RFC 1323 but tightens their wording. Appendix H lists the changes, which are partly due to errata and partly due to better understanding of how the components interact.

  • Much of the discussion in Section 1 was removed, while the examples in Sections 2, 3 and 5 were kept as guidelines.
  • Text was added that Window Scale increases the chance of sequence wrap, so PAWS is required in certain environments.
  • RFC 2119 wording was added, with specific segment types marked in angle brackets.
  • Section 3 was updated for what has been learned since RFC 1323, including that the Timestamps option must appear on every segment once negotiated.

For IANA, the Window Scale and Timestamps entries in the TCP Option Kind Numbers table now point to this document.
sections.eli5: It is a cleaned-up second edition of an older rulebook, with the unclear rules made firm.

fields.name: shift.cnt
fields.desc: Exponent of the scale factor for the sender's receive window; limited to 14.

fields.name: TS Value (TSval)
fields.desc: Current value of the sender's timestamp clock.

fields.name: TS Echo Reply (TSecr)
fields.desc: Echo of a recently received TSval; valid only when the ACK bit is set.

cells: MUST tick at least once for each 2^31 bytes sent
A clock faster than 1 tick/sec rejects old duplicates for link speeds of about 8 Gbps
Recycle time MUST be greater than the MSL
With a worst-case MSL of 255 seconds, one tick every 59 ns at most
A 1 ms clock wraps its sign bit in 24.8 days
